what: Klaviyo sells marketing software to online retailers. It connects to a shop’s e-commerce platform, builds a profile of each customer from their browsing and purchase history, and sends them email, text messages and push notifications automatically, with the revenue each message generated attributed back.
customers: Online retailers and consumer brands, from one-person Shopify shops to large multi-brand businesses. Pricing scales with the number of contacts in a customer’s database, so revenue grows as the customer grows.
money: Monthly plans priced by the size of the contact list and the volume of messages sent.
moat: Klaviyo sits on top of the shop’s own customer data, which means the longer a retailer uses it the more history it holds and the better the targeting becomes — and the more painful it is to leave. Its deep integration with Shopify made it the default for a generation of online brands. Because it attributes revenue directly to each campaign, it is measured as a profit centre rather than a cost, which is a very different budget conversation.
risks: Net income of $7.9M gives a price/earnings ratio of about 710. On reported earnings this is not a profitable company in any meaningful sense, because share-based compensation consumes the margin.
Pricing scales with contact list size, so revenue depends on customers growing. In a weak consumer environment, their lists and their sending volumes stop growing too.
Dependence on the Shopify ecosystem cuts both ways: Shopify has its own marketing tools and its interests are not permanently aligned with Klaviyo’s.
The shares trade at about 4.1 times sales, which requires growth to continue at close to the current rate.
Twenty-one analysts average a $26.98 target, about 27% above the current price, which is a modest margin for a company valued on growth.
opportunities: Revenue has grown very fast, from $290.6M in 2021 to $1.2B in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $1.5B.
Free cash flow of $245.3M is far above reported net income, because share-based compensation is a non-cash charge: the cash economics are much better than the earnings line.
Cash of $1.1B against $120.7M of debt means growth is self-funded.
Because pricing scales with list size, revenue grows from existing customers without any new sales effort — the best kind of growth there is.
Moving upmarket into larger brands raises the revenue per customer and reduces dependence on small shops.
watch: Net revenue retention. It is the one figure that captures whether existing customers are spending more each year, which is both the growth engine and the proof that the product is hard to leave.
view: Ignore the price/earnings ratio of 710. Klaviyo earned $7.9 million of accounting profit and generated $245 million of free cash flow, and the gap is almost entirely share-based compensation — a real cost to shareholders through dilution, but not a cash cost, and not something a P/E ratio handles sensibly. On free cash flow the multiple is about 24 times with $1.1 billion of net cash on the balance sheet. That is a demanding price for a software company, but it is a comprehensible one, which 710 is not.

The product is better positioned than most marketing software because of how it is bought. Klaviyo attributes revenue directly to the messages it sends, so the retailer sees it as something that generates sales rather than a cost line to be trimmed. Software sold as a profit centre survives budget cuts that destroy software sold as a cost. Combined with pricing that scales automatically with the size of the customer’s contact list, it means revenue grows from existing customers without a salesperson making a call — which is why revenue went from $291 million to $1.2 billion in four years.

The dependency that deserves the most thought is Shopify. Klaviyo’s deep integration with it made it the default for a generation of direct-to-consumer brands, and that integration is a genuine moat today. It is also a relationship with a company that sells its own marketing tools and whose interests are only temporarily aligned. Platform dependencies like this usually look like a moat right up until the platform decides otherwise, and I would want to see the share of revenue arriving from outside Shopify falling steadily.

The other side of the same coin is the macro exposure. Pricing scales with list size and sending volume, which means Klaviyo grows when its customers grow. In a weak consumer environment, small online brands do not add contacts, and some of them disappear. That makes this more cyclical than a typical subscription business, which is not how it is priced. Net revenue retention is the number that reveals both issues at once — if it stays comfortably above 100%, the product is working and the customers are healthy.
bull: Net revenue retention stays high as customers grow their lists, the move upmarket into larger brands lands, and the cash economics get recognised once share-based compensation normalises.
bear: A weak consumer environment stalls the customer lists that pricing depends on while Shopify pushes its own marketing tools, and 4 times sales meets decelerating growth.
